title: Drawing & Painting

lessons.title: Lines Go for a Walk
objectives: Draw straight, wavy, zigzag and curly lines
Combine shapes to make a picture
explanation: A line is a mark that goes from one place to another. Lines can be straight, wavy like water, zigzag like lightning, or curly like a snail's shell.
When a line goes all the way round and meets itself, it makes a shape: a circle, a square, a triangle.
Artists put lines and shapes together to make pictures. A circle and some lines can become a sun! A square and a triangle can become a house.

vocabulary.meaning: a mark from one point to another
a closed outline like a circle or square
a line with sharp ups and downs
a person who makes art

examples: Wavy lines for the sea.
A triangle on a square for a house.

story.title: The Line Who Went for a Walk
story.text: Little Line woke up on a white page and decided to go for a walk. She walked straight across the meadow, wobbled wavily over a river, zigzagged up a mountain and curled round and round into a snail shell. When she looked back, she had drawn a whole picture! "Walking is wonderful," she giggled.

lessons.title: Red, Yellow and Blue
objectives: Name the three primary colours
Mix two primary colours to make a new colour
explanation: In painting, red, yellow and blue are called primary colours. We can mix them to make many other colours.
Red and yellow make orange. Yellow and blue make green. Blue and red make purple.
Colours can make us feel things too. Bright yellow can feel happy and sunny; soft blue can feel calm.

Red and yellow making an orange sunset.

story.title: The Three Paint Pots
story.text: Three paint pots lived on a shelf: Red, Yellow and Blue. One rainy day they got bored. Yellow dripped onto Blue — and suddenly there was Green! Red splashed onto Yellow — Orange! Blue bumped into Red — Purple! "Look at all the friends we made," they laughed, painting a rainbow together.

lessons.title: Fire Colours and Ice Colours
objectives: Sort colours into warm and cool

explanation: Artists call red, orange and yellow warm colours, because they remind us of fire and sunshine. Blue, green and purple are cool colours, like water, leaves and ice.
Warm colours often seem to jump forward in a picture; cool colours seem to sit back and feel calm.
Adding white to a colour makes a lighter tint (red + white = pink). Adding black makes a darker shade.

examples: A sunset painted in warm colours.
An underwater scene in cool colours.

In the Kingdom of Ice, everything shimmered blue, green and purple, and the people were calm and quiet. One day a painter visited both and painted a picture where they met — and it was the most beautiful picture of all.

lessons.title: Rough, Smooth and Stuck Together
objectives: Describe textures using words like rough, smooth and bumpy
Make a collage using different materials
prerequisites: Can cut and glue with help
explanation: Texture is how something feels — rough like tree bark, smooth like a pebble, bumpy like a lemon, soft like wool.
Artists can show texture by making a rubbing: put paper over a leaf or coin and rub with the side of a crayon.

A collage is a picture made by sticking different materials together — paper, fabric, leaves, buttons. The French word "coller" means "to glue". Artists such as Henri Matisse made famous collages with cut paper.

vocabulary.meaning: how something feels or looks like it feels
a picture made by rubbing a crayon over a textured surface
a picture made by gluing materials together
not smooth

examples: A leaf rubbing showing veins.
A collage elephant made from grey fabric.

story.title: The Treasure Walk
story.text: Ivaan and Aaji went on a texture walk. They found rough bark, smooth stones, a fluffy feather and crinkly leaves. At home, they made rubbings and then glued everything into a collage of a magical forest. "This tree is rough because it's real bark!" Ivaan said proudly.

lessons.title: Light, Shadow and Shading
objectives: Draw an object by looking carefully
Use shading to make shapes look 3D
explanation: Observational drawing means drawing what you actually see, not what you think something looks like. Artists look at the object more than the paper.
Light makes some parts of an object bright (highlights) and other parts dark (shadows). An object also casts a shadow on the table.
Shading shows light and shadow. You can press harder for darker areas, or use hatching (lines side by side) and cross-hatching (crossed lines). Shading turns a flat circle into a round ball.

vocabulary.meaning: looking carefully
the brightest part of an object
shading with parallel lines
the shadow an object throws onto a surface

examples: Shading an apple with a highlight.
Cross-hatching the dark side of a cup.

story.title: The Apple Lesson
story.text: Kiko drew an apple as a red circle with a stalk. His art teacher placed a real apple by the window. "Look again." Kiko noticed a bright white spot, a darker side and a shadow on the table. He drew it again, shading gently. The new apple looked so round he almost wanted to bite it.

lessons.title: Warli and Madhubani
objectives: Recognise the features of Warli and Madhubani art
Create a picture inspired by a folk style, crediting its origin
explanation: Warli art comes from the Warli people of the Sahyadri region of Maharashtra. It uses simple white shapes — circles, triangles and lines — on a mud or red-brown background to show dancing, farming and village life. People are made of two triangles joined at the tip!

Madhubani (Mithila) art comes from the Mithila region of Bihar and Nepal. It traditionally was painted by women on walls, using bright colours and patterns, with every space filled with flowers, fish, birds and borders.

Other folk styles include Gond art from Madhya Pradesh (made of dots and lines) and Pattachitra from Odisha. Warli painting and Madhubani painting both have Geographical Indication (GI) tags that recognise where they come from.

vocabulary.meaning: traditional art made by communities
folk art of the Warli people of Maharashtra
folk art from the Mithila region
a repeated design

examples: The circle dance (tarpa dance) in Warli art.
Fish motifs in Madhubani paintings.

story.title: The Painted Wall
story.text: In a Warli village, Ivaan watched an artist mix rice paste with water and use a bamboo stick as a brush. On the red mud wall appeared tiny people made of triangles, dancing in a spiral around a musician. "Every picture tells about our life," the artist said. "Now you try — and remember it comes from our people."

lessons.title: The Vanishing Point
objectives: Draw a scene in one-point perspective
Use the rule of thirds to plan a composition
explanation: Perspective is a way of making a flat picture look deep. Things far away look smaller and closer together.

In one-point perspective, you draw a horizon line (where land meets sky) and a vanishing point on it. Lines going into the distance — like a road or railway — all meet at the vanishing point. Renaissance artists in Italy, such as Brunelleschi, developed this system in the 1400s.

Composition is how you arrange things in a picture. The rule of thirds divides the page into a 3×3 grid; placing important things on the lines or where they cross often looks balanced and interesting.

vocabulary.meaning: showing depth on a flat surface
where land and sky seem to meet
where parallel lines seem to meet
the arrangement of a picture

examples: Railway tracks meeting in the distance.
A tree placed on a third line in a landscape photo.

story.title: The Disappearing Road
story.text: On a long, straight road, Zuri noticed something strange: the road looked narrower and narrower until it became a single dot. The trees beside it got smaller too. "It's the vanishing point!" she said. That evening, she drew the road with a ruler, and the picture seemed to stretch for miles.

activities.prompt: Where do parallel lines meet in one-point perspective?

thinking: Why did medieval paintings often look flat?

speaking: Explain how you drew depth in your perspective scene.

lessons.title: Meet the Masters
objectives: Describe the work of four major artists
Compare artworks using art vocabulary
explanation: Raja Ravi Varma (1848–1906) from Kerala painted scenes from Indian epics in a realistic, oil-painting style. His printing press made affordable prints that spread his images of gods and heroines across India.

Amrita Sher-Gil (1913–1941), of Hungarian and Indian heritage, painted the lives of ordinary Indian women with deep, earthy colours, and is regarded as a pioneer of modern Indian art. Vincent van Gogh (1853–1890), a Dutch painter, used swirling brushstrokes and thick paint, as in "The Starry Night" (1889).
Frida Kahlo (1907–1954), from Mexico, painted bold self-portraits filled with Mexican culture and personal feelings. Each artist found their own way of seeing.

vocabulary.meaning: a picture an artist makes of themselves
a mark made by a brush
art showing things as they look
an artist's particular way of making art

examples: Ravi Varma's "Shakuntala".
Van Gogh's "Sunflowers".

story.title: A Painter With a Printing Press
story.text: In 1894, Raja Ravi Varma set up a printing press near Mumbai. Before that, most people could only see paintings in palaces. Soon, his colourful prints of Lakshmi, Saraswati and scenes from the epics hung in homes across India. A painting had travelled from the palace to the kitchen wall.

lessons.title: The Grammar of Art
objectives: Name and identify the elements and principles of art
Use colour theory, including complementary colours
explanation: The elements of art are the building blocks: line, shape, form (3D shape), colour, value (lightness and darkness), texture and space.
The principles of design are how artists arrange the elements: balance, contrast, emphasis (focal point), movement, rhythm or pattern, proportion and unity.

In colour theory, complementary colours sit opposite each other on the colour wheel — red and green, blue and orange, yellow and purple — and create strong contrast. Analogous colours sit next to each other and create harmony.

vocabulary.meaning: a basic building block of art
a way of arranging elements
colours opposite on the colour wheel
how light or dark a colour is

examples: A red flower on green leaves showing complementary contrast.
Symmetrical balance in the Taj Mahal.

story.title: Spotting the Focal Point
story.text: In a gallery, Zuri's teacher asked, "Where does your eye go first?" In the painting, a small figure in a bright orange shawl stood against a misty blue valley. "There!" said Zuri. "Exactly — complementary contrast and emphasis," the teacher said. "The artist planned that."

lessons.title: Art Movements
objectives: Describe major art movements in India and the world
Place artworks in historical context
explanation: The Ajanta cave paintings in Maharashtra, made roughly from the 2nd century BCE to the 5th century CE, show Buddhist Jataka stories. Mughal miniature painting (16th–18th centuries) combined Persian and Indian styles in fine detail.

The European Renaissance (14th–16th centuries) revived classical ideas and realism: Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo. Impressionism (1870s, France) captured light and moments with visible brushstrokes: Claude Monet's "Impression, Sunrise" gave the movement its name.

In India, the Bengal School, led by Abanindranath Tagore in the early 1900s, sought an Indian modern style. After independence, the Progressive Artists' Group (1947), including M. F. Husain, S. H. Raza and F. N. Souza, explored modernism.

vocabulary.meaning: a group of artists sharing ideas in a period
a small, detailed painting
a style capturing light and moments
art breaking with traditional styles

examples: Abanindranath Tagore's "Bharat Mata".
Monet's water lilies.

story.title: A Name From an Insult
story.text: In 1874, a critic mocked Claude Monet's painting "Impression, Sunrise", sneering that it was only an "impression", not a finished picture. The painters liked the word and kept it. Today, "Impressionism" is one of the most loved art movements in the world.

lessons.title: Four Steps of Art Criticism
objectives: Apply Feldman's four-step method of art criticism
Debate questions about the value and definition of art
explanation: Edmund Feldman proposed a four-step method: Describe (what do you see?), Analyse (how are elements and principles used?), Interpret (what does it mean or express?) and Judge (is it successful, and why?).
Context matters: knowing when, where and why a work was made can change its meaning. A work may be read differently by different audiences.

Some works challenge the idea of art itself. In 1917, Marcel Duchamp submitted a urinal titled "Fountain" to an exhibition, asking whether an artist's choice alone could make something art. Such works provoke debate about who decides what art is — artists, critics, museums or audiences.

vocabulary.meaning: a careful judgement of a work
an explanation of meaning
the circumstances in which something was made
relating to beauty and taste

examples: Interpreting Amrita Sher-Gil's "Three Girls".
Debating Duchamp's "Fountain".

story.title: The Gallery Argument
story.text: Two friends stood before a canvas painted entirely red. "Anyone could do that," said one. "But they didn't," said the other, reading the label about the artist's idea of colour and emotion. They argued all the way home — and realised that the argument itself was part of what the art was for.

lessons.title: Building Your Portfolio
objectives: Apply graphic design principles to communicate a message
Curate a portfolio that shows growth and a personal voice
explanation: Visual communication uses images, type and layout to share a message — posters, logos, book covers, infographics. Good design uses hierarchy (what to notice first), alignment, contrast and white space.
Digital tools allow layers, undo and easy sharing, but the same art principles apply. Many artists combine hand-drawn and digital work.

A portfolio is a curated collection of your best and most meaningful work. It shows skill, range, process (sketches and experiments) and a personal voice. Artists write a short artist's statement explaining their ideas and approach.

vocabulary.meaning: the order in which things are noticed
empty space in a design
a curated collection of work
a short text explaining an artist's work

examples: A poster where the title is biggest and boldest.
A portfolio page showing sketches and the final piece.

story.title: The Sketchbook That Got Her In
story.text: When Meera applied to art school, she worried her finished paintings weren't perfect. But she included her messy sketchbooks too: experiments, failures and ideas. The interviewer spent most of the time on those. "This shows how you think," he said. "That's what we're looking for."
